new_statements.translation: [p.1104] The N'Ko alphabet comprises 26 basic letters and three additional ones, seven superscript diacritics for the combined marking of tones and vowel length/shortness, and one subscript diacritic marking vowel nasality (more precisely, the nasal final element of the syllable). [p.34] Stress is absent in most Mande languages. Where it can be identified (in particular, in Bamana), its functional load is small. Tone. Practically all Mande languages are tonal...

new_statements.rule_in_words: N'Ko (the written Manding norm, phonologically = Guinean Maninka of Kankan) is described purely as a tone language: every vowel carries one of four tones (high, low, rising, high + floating low) combined with a length contrast, all obligatorily written with the seven kánmasere diacritics; no source on N'Ko or Guinean Maninka that I could open makes any statement about word stress. The only explicit stress remark found is genus-level (Vydrin 2017: 34): stress is absent in most Mande languages, identifiable (with low functional load, foot-based) mainly in Bamana — and Vydrin 2014 notes Maninka lacks the Bamana-type vowel reduction that motivates Bamana foot stress, but that inference is mine, not a published N'Ko/Maninka stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal details: word-final floating low tone ('tonal article'), downstep/downdrift, minor tonal classes (Rovenchak 2011: 85, 91-92; Diané & Vydrin 2014 sec. 3; Donaldson 2017: 149-155).
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern lexical/grammatical tone of the (orthographic) word in the N'Ko written norm = Guinean Maninka (Maninka-Mori); the p.34 stress remark is about the Mande family as a whole, not N'Ko specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: nkoa1234 'N'Ko' [nqo] is Glottolog's 'Artificial Language' entry for the written literary norm of Manding cultivated in Sulemaana Kantè's N'Ko script (kángbɛ 'clear language'); it is a second-language-only written register, not a distinct spoken vernacular. Per Davydov 2017: 164 and Vydrin & Rovenchak 2017: 1104, its de facto phonological/grammatical base is Guinean Maninka, specifically Maninka-Mori of Kankan/Baté = Eastern Maninkakan (Glottolog east2426, ISO emk), with some pan-Manding borrowings and many neologisms. Any prosodic facts for 'N'Ko' are therefore those of Guinean Maninka; the sibling audit folder holds the Maninka sources (Spears 1973, Vydrin & Diané 2014 segmental phonology, etc.).

sources.citation: Davydov, A.V. 2017. Manden dialekty Gvinei [Manding dialects of Guinea]. In: Jazyki mira: Jazyki mande. St. Petersburg: Nestor-Istorija, pp. 164-171.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.164: Maninka-Mori (Kankan/Bate) 'formed the basis of the literary Maninka language in the N'Ko tradition'; p.170: Maninka-Mori has two basic word tone patterns (H vs L/rising), tonal article.

sources.citation: Donaldson, Coleman. 2017. Clear Language: Script, Register and the N'ko Movement of Manding-Speaking West Africa. PhD dissertation, University of Pennsylvania.
sources.note: No stress statement. p.96: 'Manding is a tonal language', pitch used lexically and grammatically; pp.138-139: Kantè's kánmasere diacritics represent length and tone; pp.149-151: two tone registers H and L marked over each vowel in N'Ko, downdrift/downstep, ~90% of lexicon underlyingly H or L (citing Green 2010, Vydrin 2016).

sources.citation: Vydrin, V.F. & A.A. Rovenchak. 2017. Pis'mennosti jazykov mande [Writing systems of the Mande languages]. In: Vydrin V.F., Mazurova Ju.V., Kibrik A.A., Markus E.B. (eds.), Jazyki mira: Jazyki mande. St. Petersburg: Nestor-Istorija, pp. 1094-1112 (N'Ko alphabet section pp. 1103-1106).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.1104: N'Ko has seven superscript diacritics jointly marking tone and vowel length plus a subscript nasality dot; p.1105 Table 10 lists them (falling = H + floating L, low, high, rising + floating L, each short/long); p.1104: the de facto literary norm written in N'Ko is Guinean Maninka.

sources.citation: Vydrin, V.F. 2017. Mande jazyki [The Mande languages]. In: Jazyki mira: Jazyki mande. St. Petersburg: Nestor-Istorija, pp. 16-45.
sources.note: Family-level statement p.34: 'Stress is absent in most Mande languages; where it can be identified (in particular Bamana) its functional load is small'; foot-level stress can be spoken of in some languages, notably Bamana; practically all Mande languages are tonal. Not specific to N'Ko/Maninka.

sources.citation: Vydrin, Valentin, Andrij Rovenchak & Kirill Maslinsky. 2016. Maninka Reference Corpus: A Presentation. TALAf 2016 (JEP-TALN-RECITAL workshop), Paris. HAL halshs-01358144.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; 'In N'ko, tonal marking is obligatory on every vowel'.

sources.citation: Diané, Mamadi & Valentin Vydrin. 2014. Propositions pour l'orthographe du maninka (Guinée). Mandenkan 52: 3-21. DOI 10.4000/mandenkan.301.
sources.note: Nothing on stress ('accent' occurs only as 'accent aigu/grave' = tone diacritics). Sec.3: Maninka has hundreds of tonal minimal pairs and grammatical tone; in N'Ko tones must be carefully noted; Latin tone diacritics á high, à low, ǎ rising, â high + floating low; two major tonal classes marked on first vowel only.

sources.citation: Vydrin, Valentin. 2012. Nko, obrazovanie na jazykax manden i panmandingskoe jazykovoe edinstvo. In: Zheltov A.Ju. (ed.), Afrikanskij sbornik-2011. St. Petersburg: MAE RAN, pp. 163-178. HAL halshs-00866730.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; states that the N'Ko script 'very accurately represents the phonological system of Guinean Maninka at both the segmental and tonal levels' (sociolinguistic paper).

sources.citation: Rovenchak, Andrij. 2011. Phoneme distribution, syllabic structure, and tonal patterns in Nko texts. Mandenkan 47: 77-96. DOI 10.4000/15z7i.
sources.note: No stress statement for N'Ko/Maninka (only a passing remark p.87 that morae explain Latin stress rules). p.85: a vowel is short or long, oral or nasal, and bears one of four tones (high, low, rising, word-final floating low); 'in Nko the length is marked simultaneously with tone'; sec.5 pp.91-92 statistics of word tone patterns (H, L, LH...).

sources.citation: Vydrine, Valentin. 2010. Le Ńkó kɔ́dɔyidalan de Souleymane Kantè et la tradition lexicographique « occidentale » pour le mandingue. Mandenkan 46: 73-98. DOI 10.4000/163hm.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; section '1) La présentation des tons' (paras 42-49) compares how Kantè's monolingual N'Ko dictionary and Western Manding dictionaries note tone (Kantè gives citation forms; no underlying/surface tone distinction in the N'Ko tradition).

sources.citation: Everson, Michael, Mamady Doumbouya, Baba Mamadi Diané & Karamo Kaba Jammeh. 2004. Proposal to add the N'Ko script to the BMP of the UCS. ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2 N2765 = L2/04-172, 21 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.4: seven vowels 'each of which can bear one of seven diacritical marks which modify the tone of the vowel, and optionally a diacritical mark which indicates nasalization'; p.5 names the marks (short high, short low, short rising, long descending, long high, long low, long rising) and the high/low tone apostrophes.
